column2: On the authority of Jābir (may Allah the Exalted be pleased with him) that he heard the Prophet ﷺ say, in the year of the Conquest while he was in Makkah: “Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and His Messenger have forbidden the sale of wine, carrion, swine and idols.”
It was said: “O Messenger of Allah, what about the fat of carrion, for ships are caulked with it, hides are oiled with it, and people use it for lamps?”

He said: “No, it is unlawful.” Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said at that point: “May Allah fight the Jews! Allah forbade them the fat [of animals], so they melted it down, then sold it and consumed its price.” Recorded by al-Bukhārī and Muslim.
ʿĀm al-fatḥ (“the year of the Conquest”): the conquest of Makkah, which was in Ramaḍān in the eighth year of the Hijrah.

Ḥarrama (“have forbidden”): with the pronoun in the singular, though the context calls for the dual, indicating that the command of the Prophet ﷺ arises from the command of Allah; it is like the saying of the Exalted: “But Allah and His Messenger are more worthy that they should please Him” [al-Tawbah 9:62].
Al-maytah (“carrion”): with fatḥah on the mīm; that from which life has departed other than by lawful slaughter.
Al-aṣnām (“idols”): plural of ṣanam. Al-Jawharī said: it is the same as a wathan. Others said: a wathan is one with a body, and a ṣanam one that is a carved image.
“It is unlawful”: selling it is unlawful. Some scholars understood his words “it is unlawful” as referring to making use of it, and said that making use of it is unlawful.
Jamalūhu (“they melted it down”): they rendered it.
The prohibition of selling wine, carrion, swine and idols.
Everything whose use Allah has forbidden, its sale and consuming its price are forbidden. This is general for everything whose intended use is unlawful, and it is of two kinds.

The first is that which is used while its substance remains, such as idols, whose intended use is associating partners with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, which is the most repugnant of all sins without exception. To this are joined things whose use is unlawful, such as books of shirk, sorcery, innovation and misguidance and the like.

The second is that which can be used only by consuming its substance. If its principal intended use is unlawful, selling it is unlawful, just as selling swine, wine and carrion is unlawful, even though some of them have uses that are not unlawful,

such as eating carrion for one compelled by necessity, clearing a choking with wine, putting out a fire with it, sewing with pig's bristles and using its hair and hide. Since these uses are not the intended ones, no account is taken of them, and selling is forbidden.
Every stratagem used to make lawful what is unlawful is void.
The printed text reads المقصور, evidently for المقصود (“intended”).
